Ellasar
el-LAY-sar
proper noun
Hebrew Ellasar, a city-kingdom of Mesopotamia whose king Arioch joined the eastern coalition against the cities of the plain.

Biblical Definition

Ellasar is known only as the seat of a king in Abraham’s day. When four eastern kings marched to subdue the rebellious cities of the plain, Arioch of Ellasar rode among them: “in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations” (Gen 14:1). Again the record names him in the battle: “with Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five” (Gen 14:9). These were the great powers of the age, and they swept Sodom and Gomorrah and carried off Lot with the spoil. Then a stranger thing happened than any conquest. Abraham, with three hundred and eighteen trained servants, overtook the victorious kings, and “brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot” (Gen 14:16). Melchizedek met him with bread and wine and blessed “the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand” (Gen 14:20). Ellasar and its allies preach that the mightiest confederacy of kings is nothing before the God of Abraham. The powers of Mesopotamia mustered their chariots; one man of faith, armed with the promise, put them to flight. The battle is the LORD’s, and He delights to overturn the great by the weak that trust in Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Mesopotamian city-kingdom whose king Arioch joined the eastern coalition against Sodom (Gen 14:1,9); routed, with its allies, by Abraham and the God who delivers enemies into the hand of faith.

expand to see more

ELLASAR, a city-kingdom of Mesopotamia in the days of Abraham.

Ruled by Arioch, one of the four eastern kings (Gen 14:1).

Joined the coalition that plundered Sodom and carried off Lot.

Numbered among the four kings against five (Gen 14:9).

Routed with its allies by Abraham and the most high God (Gen 14:20).

Key Scripture

Gen 14:1 — "And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;"

Gen 14:9 — "With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five."

Gen 14:16 — "And he brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot, and his goods, and the women also, and the people."

Gen 14:20 — "And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all."

Modern Corruption

The Mesopotamian kingdom of Arioch in the eastern coalition; the entry recovers that the mightiest league of kings is nothing before the God of Abraham.

expand to see more

Ellasar figures in the first war recorded in Scripture, a coalition of great eastern powers that seemed irresistible. The lesson is not in the kingdom’s obscurity but in its defeat: the confederacy that plundered the cities of the plain was overturned by a single man of faith with three hundred and eighteen servants.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD delivers the enemies of His people into the hand of faith. The world reckons by the number of kings and the count of chariots; Abraham reckoned by the promise of God. Melchizedek blessed the most high God who had given the victory, and Abraham gave tithes of all. Ellasar and its allies stand as the first proof in Scripture that the battle is the LORD’s, and that He is pleased to scatter the mighty by the weak who trust in Him.
